title: Crown appeals decision that let cop 'drive the other way' instead of preventing suicide
article: The Crown is appealing a decision that quashed a breach of trust charge against a Toronto cop who refused to help save a young man from committing suicide.
Last month, Justice Maureen Forestell ruled Const. Kyle Upjohn won't stand trial because the officer's actions don't constitute a breach of trust.
"There was no evidence capable of" concluding he intended to commit a breach of trust, Forestell said in her decision.
A lower court committed Upjohn, 34, to stand trial in April 2017, but Forestell's decision quashed that ruling.
However, Crown law office filed an appeal Friday at the Ontario Court of Appeal, stating Forestell "misinterpreted and misapplied the law governing" the criminal intent for breach of trust.

Forestell "erred in substituting her own assessment of the evidence for that of the Justice at the preliminary inquiry and thereby exceeded the scope of her jurisdiction on review," stated an appeal by top Crown Howard Leibovich.
The prosecution seeks to have the charges reinstated.
Crown attorney Peter Scrutton argued before Forestell that Upjohn did the opposite of what police officers should do: Save people's lives.

"When Upjohn was apprised of information that someone's life was in danger, that someone needed saving and, though duty-bound to assist, did the opposite - he ignored the entreaty and literally drove the other way, apparently aimlessly for 12 minutes," Scrutton stated in his factum.
On Feb. 6, 2016, a concerned citizen told Upjohn, as he sat in his cruiser, that a young man was preparing to hang himself in High Park.
Shortly after, Alexandre Boucher, 19, was found dead.
Upjohn, a member of the service for 10 years, has been suspended since May 2016.

"This was not an innocent mistake. Upjohn masked his failure to act with dishonesty - by lying about being 'on a call.' The lie suggests that Upjohn knew what he was doing wrong, that he was intentionally using his office for a purpose other than the public good," Scrutton said.

Forestell agreed with Upjohn's lawyer Gary Clewley that the breach of trust charge did not apply because there had to be evidence that he had a corrupt or dishonest ulterior purpose for avoiding the call.
Upjohn may have "put his own comfort or needs before the good of the public," but this was "not enough" evidence to prove a breach of trust, said Forestell.
